{"result":"# The Rust Programming Language and Memory Safety

Rust is a general-purpose language designed to emphasize performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1]. Its syntax is similar to C++, but it guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector [2].

## Origins

Graydon Hoare began developing Rust in 2006, and Mozilla Research sponsored it from 2009 [2]. The language was first publicly released in 2010, and version 1.0 arrived in 2015 [2].

## What Memory Safety Means

Memory safety protects programs from bugs such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Java is memory-safe because its runtime checks array bounds and pointer dereferences [3]. By contrast, C, C++, and Fortran allow arbitrary pointer arithmetic without bounds checking, which makes them memory-unsafe [3].

## Features That Support Safety

Rust uses structs, enums, traits, and methods instead of classes or inheritance [1]. It also draws on functional ideas such as immutability, algebraic data types, and pattern matching [1].

## Conclusion

Rust shows that strong memory safety does not require a garbage collector [2]. Rust is a general-purpose language built to combine performance, type safety, concurrency, and memory safety [1]. Its syntax resembles C++, yet it avoids a garbage collector [2].

## Origins

Graydon Hoare began work on Rust in 2006, and Mozilla Research sponsored it from 2009 [2]. The language was first publicly released in 2010, and version 1.0 arrived in 2015 [2].

## What Memory Safety Means

Memory safety protects programs from bugs such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. Java achieves this partly through runtime checks on array bounds and pointer dereferences [3]. By contrast, C, C++, and Fortran permit unchecked pointer arithmetic, making them memory-unsafe [3].

## Features That Support Safety

Rust replaces classes and inheritance with structs, enums, traits, and methods [1]. It also draws on functional ideas such as immutability, algebraic data types, and pattern matching [1].

## Conclusion

Rust demonstrates that strong memory safety is achievable without a garbage collector. For programmers who need both safety and performance, that combination is the language's central appeal.
